activities.caption: erosion or deposition — file each landform
activities.name: paleoLandformSort

config.prompt: The glacier's two toolkits — file each landform:

items.label: U-shaped valley — a river valley over-deepened
cirque — armchair basin at the accumulation zone
fjord — valley scoured below sea level, then drowned
drumlin — whale-backed hill aligned with flow
erratic — boulder far from its source

config.why: Every landform is also a proxy: moraine positions map past ice extent, erratics trace flow direction — and their worldwide consistency established the glacial epochs.

activities.caption: pair each archive with what it measures
activities.name: paleoArchiveMatch

config.prompt: Each archive is an instrument — pair it with what it reads:

pairs.right: trapped bubbles — direct CO₂ and CH₄ back 800,000 years
benthic δ¹⁸O mixing temperature with global ice volume, to 100+ million years
annual, absolutely dated width and density for ~12,000 years
windblown dust — the ice ages' dry, windy continents

config.why: No single archive suffices — multi-proxy reconstruction is how the field earns its error bars, and disagreement between proxies forces better understanding of both.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — what a core actually measures
activities.name: paleoCoreSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about ice cores is backwards — click it:
lines: Annual layers count like tree rings — Greenland ice can be counted to the year.
The water's δ¹⁸O and deuterium ratio is a calibrated thermometer.
The trapped bubbles are samples of ancient air — direct CO₂ and CH₄ measurements.
The bubbles measure temperature directly, with no calibration needed.
Benthic δ¹⁸O mixes temperature with global ice volume — the two signals must be disentangled.
config.correction: Nothing in a core measures temperature directly — the proxies are isotope ratios and gas concentrations, each calibrated, corrected and cross-checked before it earns the label.
config.why: Glacial wind patterns shift the calibration and the deep-sea signal mixes ice volume — which is exactly why independent archives that disagree are made to argue.

config.prompt: From orbit to glacial maximum — put the chain in order:
items: Orbital wobbles redistribute where and when sunlight falls
Cool northern summers at 65°N let winter snow survive
Ice builds and brightens the planet — the ice–albedo feedback
Cold oceans and boreal lands absorb CO₂ — ~280 down to ~180 ppm
The greenhouse feedback deepens the cold, and dust fertilises iron-limited oceans
config.why: The orbit turns the key; CO₂, albedo and dust supply the amplitude — an astronomical metronome amplified by feedback.

activities.anchor: A proxy without a calendar is a curiosity
activities.caption: call radiocarbon's reach
activities.name: paleoC14Est

config.prompt: Of the dating toolkit, radiocarbon is the youngest-reaching — roughly how far back can it date organic material?
config.why: About 50,000 years — calibrated against tree rings because the production rate wobbles; beyond it, uranium–thorium (to ~500 kyr), volcanic layers, magnetostratigraphy and orbital tuning take over.
config.context: Layer counting stays the gold standard where annual layers exist.

activities.caption: paced change vs climate that jumps — drag the divider
activities.name: paleoJumpCompare

config.prompt: Two regimes of past climate — drag between them:

before.label: Orbitally paced change
before.text: Milankovitch rhythms of 19–100 kyr, amplified slowly by CO₂, ice–albedo and dust — the astronomical metronome.

after.label: Abrupt change
after.text: Dansgaard–Oeschger warmings of 8–16 °C within decades, ~25 through the last glacial — Atlantic circulation and sea ice flipping between modes; the Younger Dryas a 1,200-year snap back.

config.why: The Holocene's remarkable stability is not a law of nature but a fortunate regime — the same circulation levers are watched today under Greenland meltwater.

config.prompt: Sea level is the integrator that remembers — place the Last Glacial Maximum's sea level on the metres scale.
config.why: About 120 m lower: Beringia was a walkable plain and Britain joined to Europe — against +10s of metres during past warm periods.

activities.anchor: The past does not excuse the present
activities.caption: fill the blanks — natural rate vs today's
activities.name: paleoRateCloze

config.text: Natural change is paced by orbit and amplified slowly by feedbacks — about %%0%% ppm of CO₂ per thousand years. Today's rise is %%1%% ppm in a single century, carrying an isotopic %%2%%-carbon signature with no counterpart in 800,000 years of direct record.
config.hint: Both rates are in the lesson's comparison — one per millennium, one per century.
